subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]
passage: The page was called Kasba Gossip, and nobody there used real names. Lying on the charpai on the roof one night, Amandeep scrolled through a clip of Jatin from the tenth-standard function, dancing out of step. Two hundred comments already: clown faces, jokes about his stick legs. Amandeep typed as 'desi_rider09': "bro dances like a buffalo on ice." Forty laughing reactions in ten minutes. He felt a small rush, then nothing much; it was only a name on a screen, and Jatin was just pixels. Next morning at the bus stand, Jatin stood apart from everyone, hood up in the heat, staring at his shoes. Amandeep found the comment on his phone. The words looked like someone else's. They weren't.

qa.q: What name did Amandeep use to post the comment?
qa.a: Amandeep typed as 'desi_rider09'.

qa.q: What does Amandeep mean when the words look like someone else's?
qa.a: Amandeep had felt the comment belonged to the screen name, not to himself, and is now ashamed to realise it was his own cruelty after all.

qa.q: What choice could Amandeep make at the bus stand, with Jatin standing right there?
qa.a: Amandeep could delete the comment and go and speak to Jatin, owning it under his real name instead of hiding behind 'desi_rider09'.

qa.q: How does the pile-on look from where Jatin stands?
qa.a: To Jatin, two hundred comments feel like the whole kasba laughing, so he stands apart with his hood up, staring at his shoes.

grounding: Shows a teenager joining an anonymous comment pile-on because the target feels distant and the words feel like the screen name's, not his.

subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]
passage: The poll appeared in the 9B group chat at eleven at night, an anonymous one with no names shown: 'Who should just switch schools?' Mateo's name was already winning. Tomas, in his room in Valencia with the lamp off, felt the others piling in like a wave at the beach, and he wanted to be in the wave, not left on the sand. He tapped Mateo. Then, in the anonymous reply box, he added, "nobody would notice lol." It sent. No one could see it was him. For a second it was almost funny; he wasn't Tomas, he was just one vote in thirty-one. In the morning Mateo's seat by the window was empty. Tomas stared at it through the whole of maths, and the joke kept not being funny.

qa.q: What did the anonymous poll ask?
qa.a: It asked, 'Who should just switch schools?'

qa.q: Why did Tomas want to join the others?
qa.a: Tomas felt the others piling in like a wave and wanted to be in it, not left on the sand; being one vote in thirty-one made it feel less like his own act.

qa.q: What could Tomas decide once he sees the empty seat?
qa.a: Tomas could tell a teacher about the poll and message Mateo directly to apologise, making a choice as himself rather than as an anonymous vote.

qa.q: What would change if the poll had shown every voter's name?
qa.a: Tomas and many others would probably not have tapped Mateo, because each person would feel their own name attached to it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager joining an anonymous group-chat poll against a classmate because being one of many makes the act feel less his.

subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]
passage: Lights-out at Nilgiri House hostel meant the corridor turned into a dark river of boys. Tonight someone whispered that Madhav, the new boy in Room 14, had complained to the warden about the loud music. Within minutes a crowd was banging on Room 14, chanting "snitch, snitch." Darshan was at the back. In the dark he couldn't see faces, and nobody could see his. He banged too, harder than he meant, his palm stinging. It felt as if the corridor was doing it, not him. Then the tubelight flickered on. Suddenly there were just twenty ordinary boys in vests and shorts, and Darshan, with his hand still raised against a door he had never even knocked on before. Inside, Madhav's radio clicked off.

qa.q: What was the crowd chanting at Room 14?
qa.a: They were chanting "snitch, snitch."

qa.q: What did Darshan feel while he banged in the dark?
qa.a: Darshan felt carried along and free of blame, as if the corridor was doing it, not him, because in the dark nobody could see his face.

qa.q: What is the turning point for Darshan, and what could he choose next?
qa.a: When the tubelight flickers on, Darshan sees himself as one ordinary boy with his hand raised; he could lower it, walk away, and later speak to Madhav.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhav inside Room 14?
qa.a: For Madhav, a crowd he cannot see is banging and chanting, with no single person to talk to, so he goes silent and his radio clicks off.

grounding: Shows a hostel boy joining a dark-corridor mob and feeling the act is the crowd's, until the light makes him an individual again.

subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]
passage:
Dear Rajni,

I'm writing this instead of saying it, because I'm a coward about saying it.

Last Friday, when the anonymous school confessions page posted the clip of you singing at the assembly, the comments were already crazy. Hundreds. Everyone was adding something. I scrolled for ten minutes and then I added one too, under a made-up name. It was mean. I won't repeat it.

I keep trying to explain how it felt. It didn't feel like me typing. You felt far away, like a picture, and everyone else was doing it, so it seemed like just one more drop in the rain. But it was my thumb. On Monday I saw you eat lunch alone in the library, and I knew which drop was mine.

I've deleted it. I'm sorry. Your high note was actually good.

Jasleen (the girl two rows behind you in maths)

qa.q: Where did Jasleen see Rajni eating lunch on Monday?
qa.a: Jasleen saw Rajni eat lunch alone in the library.

qa.q: Why did posting the comment not feel like her own action to Jasleen at the time?
qa.a: Rajni felt far away like a picture, the name was made up and everyone else was commenting, so it felt like one more drop in the rain.

qa.q: What choice did Jasleen make after Monday, and what could she add to it?
qa.a: She deleted the comment and wrote to apologise; she could also report the clip to a teacher so the page takes it down.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Rajni may feel a mix of hurt and relief, hurt to know a classmate joined in, but glad someone admitted it and praised Rajni's high note.

grounding: A teenager joins a cruel comment pile-on under a made-up name because the target feels distant and everyone is doing it, and later owns it.

subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]
passage: "You want the embarrassing one, Aadhya? Fine, this is Yash at his worst. Last year I played this online shooting game every night in a voice lobby, all random usernames, nobody's real face. One night a player on our team kept dying early. Someone started calling him useless, then another person, then all five of us. I joined in. I said things I would never say to anyone at school, and it felt like nothing, like I was just part of the noise and he was just a username. Then he unmuted to reply and his voice cracked. He sounded about twelve. He said, 'Sorry, I'm new.' Everyone laughed and kept going. I left the game. I sat there with my headset in my lap feeling sick. The worst part? For those ten minutes, I honestly hadn't felt like it was me."

qa.q: How many people in the lobby were calling the player useless?
qa.a: All five of them, including Yash, were calling him useless.

qa.q: What made Yash feel sick with the headset in his lap?
qa.a: Hearing the player's cracked, young-sounding voice made the target suddenly real, and Yash realised the cruelty had been his even though it felt like just noise.

qa.q: What could Yash do the next time a lobby starts piling on someone?
qa.a: He could stay quiet or say one plain line such as 'leave him, he's new,' and mute or report the players who keep going, instead of joining in.

qa.q: What was that night like for the new player?
qa.a: He was a young beginner who apologised and was laughed at by five strangers at once, with no one to reason with.

grounding: A teenager in an anonymous gaming lobby joins a pile-on because everyone is doing it and the target feels distant, and only later feels it was his.
